```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
int <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
```

With the [fundamental counting principle](../counting-principle/index.qmd) we saw that 3 different prizes can go to 10 people in $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8$ ways. Products like this appear whenever we **put things in order**, so they deserve formulas of their own. Combinatorics distinguishes three ways of counting:

- **permutations:** put *all* the elements of a set in order,
- **arrangements** (k-permutations): choose $k$ elements and put them in order,
- **combinations:** choose $k$ elements without caring about order.

In permutations and arrangements **order matters**: $(\alpha, \beta)$ differs from $(\beta, \alpha)$. Today we cover these two; combinations come in the next post.

## Permutations

A **permutation** of the $n$ elements of a set is any way of putting them in a row. The first position can be filled in $n$ ways, the second in $n - 1$, …, the last in 1, so

$$(n)_n = n \cdot (n-1) \cdots 2 \cdot 1 = n!.$$

The permutations of $\{\alpha, \beta, \gamma\}$ number $3! = 6$: $\alpha\beta\gamma$, $\alpha\gamma\beta$, $\beta\alpha\gamma$, $\beta\gamma\alpha$, $\gamma\alpha\beta$, $\gamma\beta\alpha$. Ten students can sit in a row in $10! =$ `r int(factorial(10))` ways. The factorial grows explosively: a 52-card deck can be shuffled in $52! \approx 8 \cdot 10^{67}$ ways, so almost surely every good shuffle produces an order that has never appeared before.

### Permutations with repeated elements

What if some elements are identical? If we tell the two Bs of A, B, B apart as $\text{B}_1$ and $\text{B}_2$, the $3! = 6$ permutations give the same word in pairs. There are $6 / 2! = 3$ distinct words: ABB, BAB, BBA.

More generally, if the $n$ elements fall into $m$ groups of identical elements of sizes $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_m$ ($s_1 + \cdots + s_m = n$), the number of distinct permutations is

$$\frac{n!}{s_1! \cdot s_2! \cdots s_m!}.$$

The word STATISTICS has 10 letters: S three times, T three times, I twice, A and C once. It has $10!/(3! \cdot 3! \cdot 2!) =$ `r int(factorial(10) / (6 * 6 * 2))` anagrams. Type your own word into the explorer:

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Anagram explorer
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof word17 = Inputs.text({label: "Word", value: "STATISTICS", maxlength: 14})
viewof shuffle17 = Inputs.button("Random anagram")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  shuffle17;
  const w = [...word17.normalize("NFD").replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, "").toUpperCase()].filter(c => /\p{L}/u.test(c));
  if (w.length === 0) return html`<div class="ix-note">Type a word.</div>`;
  const fact = n => { let r = 1n; for (let i = 2n; i <= BigInt(n); i++) r *= i; return r; };
  const counts = d3.rollups(w, v => v.length, c => c).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
  const denom = counts.reduce((p, [, s]) => p * fact(s), 1n);
  const distinct = fact(w.length) / denom;
  const nf = x => BigInt(x).toLocaleString("en-GB");
  const sh = d3.shuffle(w.slice()).join("");
  // list every distinct anagram when there are few
  let list = null;
  if (distinct <= 720n) {
    const out = [], cnt = new Map(counts);
    const rec = (pref) => {
      if (pref.length === w.length) { out.push(pref.join("")); return; }
      for (const [c, s] of cnt) if (s > 0) { cnt.set(c, s - 1); pref.push(c); rec(pref); pref.pop(); cnt.set(c, s); }
    };
    rec([]);
    list = out;
  }
  const chips = counts.map(([c, s]) => html`<span style="display:inline-block;border:1px solid ${s > 1 ? "#f28e2b" : "#9ecae1"};background:${s > 1 ? "#fff4e8" : "#f3f8fc"};border-radius:12px;padding:1px 9px;margin:2px">${c} × ${s}</span>`);
  const rep = counts.filter(([, s]) => s > 1);
  const formula = rep.length ? `${w.length}! / (${rep.map(([, s]) => s + "!").join(" · ")})` : `${w.length}!`;
  return html`<div>${chips}</div>
    <table class="ix-tbl">
      <tr><td>Letters</td><td><b>${w.length}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Permutations if all were different</td><td><b>${w.length}! = ${nf(fact(w.length))}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Each word is repeated</td><td><b>${nf(denom)}</b> times</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Distinct anagrams</td><td><b>${formula} = ${nf(distinct)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>A random one</td><td><b>${sh}</b></td></tr>
    </table>
    ${list ? html`<div class="ix-note">All the anagrams:</div><div style="max-height:160px;overflow-y:auto;font-family:monospace;font-size:0.9em;line-height:1.6;border:1px solid #dde3ea;border-radius:6px;padding:4px 8px">${list.join(" · ")}</div>` : html`<div class="ix-note">Try a short word (e.g. ABB or MAMA) to see every anagram.</div>`}`;
}
```
:::

## Arrangements

An **arrangement** of $n$ elements **taken $k$ at a time** ($k \le n$), also called a $k$-permutation, is any way of choosing $k$ different elements and putting them in order. The first position has $n$ choices, the second $n - 1$, …, the $k$-th $n - k + 1$:

$$P(n, k) = n \cdot (n-1) \cdots (n-k+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}.$$

The arrangements of $\{\alpha, \beta, \gamma\}$ two at a time number $P(3, 2) = 6$: $\alpha\beta$, $\beta\alpha$, $\alpha\gamma$, $\gamma\alpha$, $\beta\gamma$, $\gamma\beta$. Permutations are the special case $k = n$, since $P(n, n) = n!$.

If **repetition** is allowed, every position always has $n$ choices and there are $n^k$ arrangements. For $\{\alpha, \beta, \gamma\}$ two at a time with repetition there are $3^2 = 9$, since $\alpha\alpha$, $\beta\beta$, $\gamma\gamma$ are added.

**Example.** We pick a random 4-digit code. What is the probability that all its digits differ? All codes are arrangements with repetition, $10^4$. The favourable ones are arrangements without repetition, $P(10, 4) = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7$:

```{r}
#| label: code-distinct
P <- function(n, k) prod(n:(n - k + 1))
P(10, 4) / 10^4
```

That is `r pct(P(10, 4) / 10^4)`. In R we can also check the formulas by listing. For the arrangements of $\{1, \ldots, 5\}$ two at a time:

```{r}
#| label: list-arrangements
g <- expand.grid(first = 1:5, second = 1:5)
c(with_rep = nrow(g), without_rep = sum(g$first != g$second), formula = P(5, 2))
```

## The birthday problem

There are 20 people in a room. What is the probability that at least two share a birthday? We ignore 29 February and treat the 365 days as equally likely.

All possible sequences of birthdays number $365^{20}$, arrangements with repetition. It is easier to count the complement $A'$: "everyone has a different birthday". Its favourable cases are arrangements without repetition, $P(365, 20)$. So

$$P(A) = 1 - \frac{P(365, 20)}{365^{20}} = 1 - \frac{365 \cdot 364 \cdots 346}{365^{20}}.$$

```{r}
#| label: birthday
p_shared <- function(n) 1 - prod((365 - n + 1):365) / 365^n
p_shared(20)
# base R has a ready-made function
pbirthday(20)
# simulate 10,000 rooms
mean(replicate(10000, any(duplicated(sample(365, 20, replace = TRUE)))))
```

The probability is `r pct(p_shared(20))`: in 100 groups of 20 people we expect about 41 to contain a shared birthday. Intuition usually fails here because we think "someone with *my* birthday". The problem asks about **any pair**, and 20 people form 190 pairs. With just `r min(which(sapply(1:100, p_shared) > 0.5))` people the probability already exceeds 50%.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
The birthday problem
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof n17 = Inputs.range([2, 80], {label: "People in the room", step: 1, value: 20})
viewof room17 = Inputs.button("New room")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pShared17 = n => { let q = 1; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) q *= (365 - i) / 365; return 1 - q; }
{
  room17;
  const days = Array.from({length: n17}, () => 1 + Math.floor(365 * Math.random()));
  const cnt = d3.rollup(days, v => v.length, d => d);
  const dots = [];
  const seen = new Map();
  days.forEach(d => { const k = (seen.get(d) || 0); seen.set(d, k + 1); dots.push({day: d, level: k, shared: cnt.get(d) > 1}); });
  const nShared = [...cnt.values()].filter(v => v > 1).length;
  const months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"];
  const starts = [1, 32, 60, 91, 121, 152, 182, 213, 244, 274, 305, 335];
  const strip = Plot.plot({
    width: 640, height: 90, marginLeft: 10, marginRight: 10,
    x: {domain: [1, 366], ticks: starts, tickFormat: (d, i) => months[i], label: null},
    y: {domain: [0, 3], axis: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#ccc"}),
      Plot.dot(dots, {x: "day", y: d => d.level + 0.5, r: 4, fill: d => d.shared ? "#f28e2b" : "#4e79a7"})
    ]
  });
  const curve = d3.range(1, 81).map(n => ({n, p: pShared17(n)}));
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: 640, height: 220, marginLeft: 45,
    x: {label: "People →", domain: [1, 80]},
    y: {label: "↑ P(shared birthday)", domain: [0, 1], grid: true, tickFormat: "%"},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#c62828", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "n", y: "p", stroke: "#4e79a7", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot([{n: n17, p: pShared17(n17)}], {x: "n", y: "p", r: 6, fill: "#f28e2b"})
    ]
  });
  const fmtP = x => x.toLocaleString("en-GB", {style: "percent", minimumFractionDigits: 1, maximumFractionDigits: 1});
  return html`${strip}
    <div class="ix-note">${nShared > 0 ? html`<span style="color:#c25e00"><b>${nShared}</b> ${nShared === 1 ? "day has" : "days have"} a shared birthday (orange).</span>` : html`Everyone in this room has a different birthday.`}
    Pairs of people: <b>${(n17 * (n17 - 1) / 2).toLocaleString("en-GB")}</b>.</div>
    ${chart}
    <table class="ix-tbl"><tr><td>P(at least two share a birthday) for ${n17} people</td><td><b>${fmtP(pShared17(n17))}</b></td></tr></table>`;
}
```
:::

Press "New room" a few times with 23 people: about half of the rooms show orange dots. With 50 people, almost always.

## Key takeaways

- **Permutations** of $n$ elements: $n!$. With groups of identical elements: $n!/(s_1! \cdots s_m!)$.
- **Arrangements** of $n$ taken $k$ at a time: $P(n, k) = n!/(n-k)!$ without repetition, $n^k$ with repetition.
- Order matters in both. When it does not, we are talking about combinations.
- In the **birthday problem** we count the complement: with 23 people the chance of a shared birthday exceeds 50%.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz17 = [
  {q: "Eight runners take part in a race. In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded?",
   opts: ["24", "56", "336", "512"], ans: 2,
   why: "Arrangements of 8 taken 3 at a time without repetition: P(8, 3) = 8 · 7 · 6 = 336. Order matters because the medals differ."},
  {q: "How many anagrams does the word MAMA have?",
   opts: ["4", "6", "12", "24"], ans: 1,
   why: "4 letters, with M and A twice each: 4! / (2! · 2!) = 24 / 4 = 6. Check them in the explorer."},
  {q: "Three siblings share 4 tablets, one each. In how many ways can they do it?",
   opts: ["4", "12", "24", "64"], ans: 2,
   why: "Arrangements of 4 taken 3 at a time: P(4, 3) = 4 · 3 · 2 = 24."},
  {q: "A die is rolled 6 times. What is the probability that all 6 numbers appear?",
   opts: ["1/6", "6!/6⁶ ≈ 1.5%", "1/6⁶", "6/6⁶"], ans: 1,
   why: "There are 6⁶ = 46,656 sequences. The favourable ones are the permutations of the 6 numbers, 6! = 720. So 720 / 46,656 ≈ 1.54%."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz17.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz17.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** (a) How many "words" can be written with all the letters of PEPPER? (b) How many of them start with PP? (c) What is the probability that a random one does not start with PP?

**3.** Ten students sit in a row at random. What is the probability that the two youngest sit next to each other?

**4.** Use `p_shared()` (or `pbirthday()`) to find how many people are needed for the probability of a shared birthday to exceed 90%.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. (a) 6 letters, with P three times and E twice: $6!/(3! \cdot 2!) = 60$. (b) The letters P, E, E, R remain for 4 positions: $4!/2! = 12$. (c) $1 - 12/60 = 4/5 = 80\%$.
3. The two youngest take two adjacent seats: 9 pairs of seats, times 2 for their order within the pair. The other 8 sit in $8!$ ways. So $\dfrac{9 \cdot 2 \cdot 8!}{10!} = \dfrac{18}{90} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.
4. `min(which(sapply(1:100, p_shared) > 0.9))` gives `r min(which(sapply(1:100, p_shared) > 0.9))` people.
:::
